title: Army invokes emergency powers to detonate lead in Iowa, bypass court order
byline: By Jack Queen and Jim Urquhart

content_html:
By Jack Queen and Jim Urquhart

AUGUSTA, Iowa, Nov 22 (Reuters) - The US Army will detonate 68 barrels of a toxic lead explosive in Iowa this week on emergency legal powers that allow it to bypass a court order blocking the controversial plan, the Trump administration told a court this ‌weekend.

The US Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit temporarily halted the detonation by freezing the Army's environmental permit on Thursday after environmental groups sued to ‌halt the operation. The government said in Saturday night's filing that the Army plans to move forward without a permit by invoking an emergency munitions and explosives exception to federal environmental protection laws.

Federal officials say the ​detonation must go forward within the next several days because a drop in temperature could destabilize the material and cause an uncontrolled explosion.

"The Army must perform a controlled detonation to protect the public from the more significant threat from an uncontrolled explosion," the Justice Department said in a court filing late on Saturday.

The Army had previously postponed plans to detonate the degraded lead azide, an explosive used in military munitions, after public outcry by residents and farmers near Middletown, Iowa.

The Justice Department said the Army would act by Tuesday, November ‌24. The Army later said in a post on ⁠X on Sunday the detonation would take place on Wednesday, November 25, "to allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced."

The Army did not respond to a Reuters inquiry on Sunday about the precise timing of the detonation. "Additional details on this situation will ⁠be forthcoming," the Army said in its X post.

DETAILS SOUGHT

Lead exposure can cause serious health problems, particularly in children, including damage to the brain and nervous system.

The Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club's Iowa chapter filed the lawsuit challenging the detonation, arguing that the detonations would release a toxic plume of lead dust into the air that could travel 100 miles (160 km) ​north ​of the site, depending on weather conditions.

Kerri Johannsen, senior director of policy and programs at the ​Iowa Environmental Council, told Reuters the Army should provide more details ‌about the timing of the detonation, where the plume is expected to travel, and what precautions people should take.

"One of the pieces that especially raised our concerns was the lack of prior notice and the fact that many folks, including state officials, did not have any heads-up about this… There was not enough information being shared," Johannsen said.

The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship has recommended that cattle farmers near the detonation site move their livestock, feed and equipment indoors or transport them to alternate locations. But farmers have told the environmental council that keeping livestock indoors is not a viable option, Johannsen said.

In a statement on Thursday, acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle ‌said the Army had determined with the US Environmental Protection Agency that a controlled detonation ​to dispose of the degraded lead was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public.

Still, ​the Army advised people to avoid the affected area during the detonation and ​urged anyone who could not leave beforehand to stay indoors, close windows and doors and shut off heating and cooling systems that ‌bring in outside air. Residents should wet-clean surfaces children may touch ​to remove any lead dust once the exposure ​period has ended, the Army said.

"The early recommendations from the Army had a lot of people sort of with their jaws hanging open … There remain so many questions about mitigation and protection," Johannsen said.

Jeremy Atwater, a resident of Augusta, Iowa, said he planned to head west because he expected the plume ​would blow south through his town.

"Anything but the bomb," Atwater ‌told Reuters outside his home, as a set of two green swings in his yard swayed in the wind. "It's just going to be a ​big problem."

(Reporting by Jack Queen in New York and Jim Urquhart in Augusta, Iowa; additional reporting by Ashraf Fahim in Washington and Luc Cohen ​in New York; Editing by Sergio Non, Bill Berkrot, Stephen Coates and Lincoln Feast.)
